title: Trump Grants Posthumous Pardon to Pete Rose, MLB’s All‑Time Hits Leader – NBC News
body:
Former baseball legend Pete Rose received a posthumous presidential pardon on Thursday, when former President Donald J. Trump used his social‑media platform to announce a “complete and total” clemency for the late player. Rose, who died earlier this year at 77, had been barred from Major League Baseball for life after an investigation revealed he bet on games he was involved in. The pardon, granted more than three decades after Rose’s 1990 guilty plea to federal tax‑evasion charges, marks an unprecedented gesture that has reignited debate over the integrity of the sport and the political use of presidential pardons.

Rose’s career remains one of baseball’s most storied achievements. Over 24 seasons, he amassed 4,256 hits, a record that still stands as the most in MLB history. His relentless drive on the field earned him a place in the Hall of Fame’s “players” ballot for years, but the betting scandal—uncovered by a 1989 investigation—led to his lifetime ban in 1989 and a subsequent conviction for filing false income tax returns. The ban prevented Rose from ever being considered for induction into the Hall of Fame, a point of contention among fans and former players who argue that his on‑field accomplishments should outweigh his off‑field transgressions.

Trump’s decision to pardon Rose comes amid a broader pattern of the former president’s use of executive clemency to reward individuals he perceives as having been wronged by the establishment. Critics argue that the move is more symbolic than substantive, noting that Rose has been dead for nearly three months and that a pardon cannot restore his eligibility for Hall of Fame induction, which is governed by separate voting rules. Nonetheless, supporters claim the pardon serves as a moral vindication, signaling that Rose’s gambling was a personal failing rather than a criminal act deserving of lifelong exile from the sport.

Legal scholars point out that a presidential pardon, even when issued posthumously, carries no practical effect on a deceased person’s record beyond removing the legal stain of conviction. “The pardon erases the legal consequences of the tax‑evasion conviction, but it does not rewrite baseball’s disciplinary decisions,” said Professor Elaine Martinez of the Sports Law Institute at Georgetown University. “The MLB’s ban is a private‑sector sanction, and the Hall of Fame’s voting procedures remain unchanged. The pardon is largely a political statement.”

The reaction from the baseball community has been mixed. Former teammates and rivals, including Hall of Famers Cal Ripken Jr. and Tony Gonzalez, expressed cautious optimism, noting that Rose’s contributions to the game deserve recognition. In contrast, former commissioner Bud Selig’s former deputy, former MLB commissioner Rob Manfred, warned that “the integrity of the sport depends on consistent enforcement of its rules,” implying that any reconsideration of Rose’s status would require a formal review by baseball’s governing bodies.

Looking ahead, the pardon may prompt renewed discussions about the criteria for Hall of Fame induction and whether the league should revisit its lifetime ban policy. Some advocacy groups have already filed petitions urging MLB to re‑examine the case, citing the pardon as evidence that public sentiment is shifting. Whether the league will act on those calls remains uncertain, but the episode underscores how political gestures can intersect with sports governance, potentially reshaping the legacy of one of baseball’s most polarizing figures.
